akṣayya
(‘imperishable’)
------------------------------------------
Performance of religious rites to appease or please the ancestors is an integral part of हिन्दुइस्म्. During such ceremonies called ‘śrāddha,’ appropriate mantras (incantations) are chanted. One of those mantras containing the wish that the offerings be imperishable, chanted by the performer of the rite, is known as ‘akṣayya’ or ‘akṣayyasthāna.’ The form of the मन्त्र is as follows: ‘Om, adya amukagotrasya pituḥ amukaśarmaṇe datta-tadannapanādikam akṣayyamastu,’ ‘May the ड़ोओद् and drink given by (me) to so and so, of such and such गोत्र, on this day, become imperishable.’ (vide Yājña-valkya Smṛti, Śrāddhaprakaraṇam, 243, [Commentary] Vīramitrodaya.)

Akṣayya-tṛtīyā
(‘the inexhaustible third day’)
------------------------------------------
Festivals and sacred days exist in all religions. They are usually the days associated with holy persons or memorable events. अक्षय्य-तृतीया which falls on the 3rd day of śuklapakṣa (bright fortnight) of the month of Vaiśākha (April-May) is said to be the day on which the कृतयुग (the first of the four युगस् or ages) began. Its name is derived from the fact that it falls on the third day of the lunar चलेन्दर् month (tṛtīyā = the 3rd) and the religious merit acquired on this day becomes in-exhaustible (akṣaya).
Fasting, worship of Lord वासुदेव with whole grains of rice, study of Vedic texts, recitation of mantras, performance of होम (offerings into consecrated fire), offerings to the departed manes, gifts to brāhmaṇas—these are some of the observances recommended.
Many tradesmen begin their new-year’s business on this day.
This is one of the days considered to be extremely auspicious during the year.

Akṣi Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is one of the minor उपनिषद्स् belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.
It starts with the visit of the sage Sāṅkṛti to Ādityaloka, the world of आदित्य or Sun-god, and pleasing him with a laudatory hymn. This hymn has been called ‘cākṣuṣmatī-विद्या.’ The Sun-god who is the deity presiding over light in the external world and the power of sight in the bodies of living beings, declares that whosoever recites this hymn regularly everyday will not be affected by diseases of the eye. Since this Upaniṣad thus begins with a hymn connected with the ‘akṣi’ or the eye, it has been named Akṣi Upaniṣad.
The sage Sāṅkṛti then beseeches Lord आदित्य to teach him ब्रह्मविद्या or knowledge of ब्रह्मन्. This question leads to a fairly long discourse by आदित्य on quite a few of the well-known Vedāntic doctrines. A major part of this is devoted to a description of the seven bhūmis or planes of yogic state.
In the first state, the योगि looks upon everything as the one, the unborn, indestructible, eternal Principle. This gradually leads to a natural dissolution of the मिन्द् wherein nothing except that one, is experienced. This is योग. Trying to remain in that state, the योगि performs all actions. He is detached from all the internal mental impressions, but performs all good actions, actions which will not cause agitation in others’ minds. He loves all and speaks words suitable for the time and place. He serves the holy ones in all ways. He is interested in reflecting upon the holy scriptures.
In the second state, the योगि approa-ches people well-versed in the scriptures and learns from them about śrutis (Vedas), smṛtis (secondary scriptures), सदाचार (good conduct) and yogic practices like धारणा (attention) and ध्यान (meditation). He tries to transcend the six evils like pride and greed.
In the third state he fixes his मिन्द् on the truths of the scriptures after hearing about them from the ṛṣis in the वानप्रस्थ stage of life. He observes hard austerities like lying on a bed of stone and roaming in the forests, to develop non-attachment. He develops great detachment to all the things of life—pairs of opposite—taking them as either due to the previous कर्म or as the will of God.
In the fourth state, the योगि has transcended duality, is established in the advaita or non-dual state of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and hence perceives the world only as a dream.
In the fifth state, even this perception of the world as a dream disappears.
In the sixth state, his मिन्द् gets attenuated further, advaitic चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् becomes stronger, and doubts and bonds disappear. He is, for all practical purposes, a jīvanmukta or ‘one who is liberated even while living.’
The seventh state, which the Upaniṣad call s as ‘videhamukti’ is characterized by total freedom from all bonds, rules and regulations and deep constant experience of the highest identity with परमात्मन् or वासुदेव, the Supreme God.
See also UPANIṢADS.

akṣapaṭala
(‘depository of legal documents’)
------------------------------------------
A study of the Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य (400 B. C.-A.

) reveals that the administration of a State was fairly well-organized even from the modern stan-dards. One of the departments described in detail is the ‘akṣapaṭala,’ the department which preserved legal documents and records of accounts. The doors of this office building faced north or east with rooms for the clerical staff and sufficient accommodation for account books and documents. The adhyakṣa (superintendent) of this section had to maintain strictly all accounts pertaining to taxes, dues and fines and take measures to prevent embezzlement of State funds. It was also his duty to maintain a register of the धर्म (customs, usages, methods of judicial procedures) of the various caste groups, families and corporations.

akṣara
(‘imperishable’)
------------------------------------------
Literally the word signifies anything that is not क्षर, not destructible, hence imperishable. The उपनिषद्स् use it to describe ब्रह्मन् or even as its synonym. For example: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.8.8, 9, 10 and 11; Kaṭha 3.2; Muṇḍaka

and so on. It is for this reason that the Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य् uses the word as one of the many names of शिव and विष्णु.
Akṣara also signifies प्रणव or Om, the monosyllable that stands for the highest ब्रह्मन् (vide Bhagavadgītā 8.13).
The word is also widely used to indicate the letters of the Sanskrit alphabet.

Akṣayavaṭa
(‘the imperishable Banyan tree’)
------------------------------------------
Performing the śrāddha (obsequial ceremony) at गया (the famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे in Bihar) has been a very ancient custom. One of the places where such śrāddha can be performed in गया is the अक्षयवट, a huge Banyan tree considered to be extremely ancient. If piṇḍas (obsequial offering of rice balls) are offered under this tree to the departed ancestors, they are believed to enjoy its fruits eternally. Hence the appellation ‘akṣaya’ (= imperishable; hence, eternal).
The śrāddha at the अक्षयवट is to be performed on the northern side at its bottom. Honouring the ब्राह्मणस् who assist in the ceremony and bowing to the tree itself are important aspects of this ritual.
There is another अक्षयवट in प्रयाग (modern Allahabad in Uttar Pradesh). Death at its foot is considered to ensure attainment of the city of विष्णु.
One more अक्षयवट exists at काशी.

akṣimocana
(‘liberating the eyes’)
------------------------------------------
Temples are an integral part of Hindu religion and culture. The building of a temple is considered a very sacred act. It is built according to a plan and pattern as given in the आगमस्. The image of the Chief Deity installed in the main shrine (garbhagṛha) is the central focus of the whole temple complex. This image is prepared strictly according to the rules of the mūrtiśilpaśāstras, works of Hindu इचोनोग्रफ्य्. Normally, even after completing the sculpturing of the image, its eyes will not be ‘opened.’ This has to be done ceremonially before installing it. This process is called ‘akṣimocana’ or ‘netronmīlana.’
The image is first placed on the स्थण्डिल (ground specially prepared for the purpose). The śilpi (sculptor) works on the eye with a golden needle opening the sight. After honouring him and bidding farewell the image is cleansed with five kinds of earth and five products of the cow (pañcagavya). It is then established on another स्थण्डिल with grains spread over. A brief worship is performed with गन्ध (sandal paste) and the image sprinkled with honey, milk and ghee. The sun, मोओन् and fire are invoked into the (three) eyes. Finally it is bathed in scented water.

akṣayapātra
(‘inexhaustible bowl’)
------------------------------------------
After losing the game of dice, when युधिष्ठिर (the eldest of the Pāṇḍava princes) was living in exile in the forest Kāmyaka, he found it impossible to feed the ever increasing number of guests. Then he prayed to सूर्य (the sun God) and obtained the अक्षयपात्र, a bowl which could supply any quantity of ड़ोओद् until द्रौपदी ate from it (vide महाभारत, Vanaparva, ch. 1).

Akṣapāda
(‘One who has an eye in his foot’)
------------------------------------------
Akṣapāda is identified with गौतम, the founder of the न्याय-दर्शन (the न्याय system of philosophy, of logical realism) and might have lived in the 3rd century B. C. The story goes that he was cross with व्यास who had criticised his philosophy and so vowed that he would never see him. Later on, realizing his mistake he produced through his yogic powers an eye in his foot through which he could see व्यास but could also maintain the earlier vow of not seeing him with the regular eyes.
See also GAUTAMA and NYĀYA-DARŚANA.

Akṣamālikā Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Classed under the Śaiva उपनिषद्स् (Upaniṣads dealing with the aspects connected with शैविस्म्) and belonging to the Ṛgveda, the Akṣamālikā Upaniṣad is a minor work in prose. It deals with the ritual consecration of a जपमाला or rosary. It is in the form of a dialogue between प्रजापति and गुह (also known as स्कन्द, कार्त्तिकेय and सुब्रह्मण्य, son of पार्वती and शिव), the latter being the preceptor.
The जपमाला can be made of beads of ten substances: coral, pearl, quartz, conch, silver, gold, sandalwood, seeds of putrajīvikā (Roxburghii), seeds of lotus and रुद्राक्ष (Elaeocarpus seeds). The string that holds them together can be made of gold, silver and copper, the three wires being twisted into one.
The Upaniṣad then gives the process of contemplation on various deities like ब्रह्मा, विष्णु, शिव and सरस्वती as situated in the various parts of the जपमाला. This is followed by a ritualistic process of cleansing the जपमाला with पञ्चगव्य, the five products of a cow like milk and curds. (See PAÑCAGAVYA.) Then comes a long section describing the infusing of each of the beads with the power of the deities presiding over the fifty alphabets of the सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे, by relating one bead with one letter of the alphabet. This is repeated again after 50 beads. The appropriate mantras or esoteric formulae to be used are also given.
After this, prayers are offered to the deities residing on earth, in the sky and in हेअवेन्, as also to the पितृस् or manes, to reside in the beads and make the जपमाला holy and effective.
The Upaniṣad ends with prayer to the rosary thus consecrated and a eulogy of this science given in it.
See also JAPAMĀLĀ and UPANIṢADS.

akṣamālā
(‘rosary of रुद्राक्ष beads’)
------------------------------------------
Japa or repetition of a मन्त्र (a set religious formula or a name of God or of a deity) is considered an important aspect of spiritual and religious discipline. Since a count of such repetition should be kept, devices for keeping such count are common to all religions. One important device is the mālā or rosary.
A rosary made of रुद्राक्ष beads called अक्षमाला (Elaeocarpus ganitrus or its berries) is very common. The number of beads may vary: 32, 54, 64 or 108. There will be one bead extra, which will be bigger than the others or fixed above the others. This is called ‘meru’ and should not be crossed over during counting.
Certain icons of gods (for e. g., शिव, सरस्वती, ब्रह्मा) are shown with the अक्षमाला in one of their hands.
Vasiṣṭha’s wife अरुन्धती is sometimes known as अक्षमाला.
See also JAPAMĀLĀ.

Akṣipuruṣa-vidyā
(‘Science of the person in the eye’)
------------------------------------------
Indian philosophical thought has reached its acme in the उपनिषद्स्. Coming as a reaction to Vedic ritualism and priestcraft it had to stress the need for realizing the spiritual dimensions of man. The sages of the उपनिषद्स्, with their deep insight into human nature, knew that a total break with the past would be rather difficult for the men steeped lifelong in rituals. Wishing to lead them to higher levels of spiritual experience, step by step, these sages devised several upāsanās or विद्यास् (mystic meditations) often based on the same rituals which they practised.
One of these विद्यास् that occurs in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (4.15 and 8.7.4) is the Akṣipuruṣavidyā. ‘Akṣipuruṣa’ means ‘the person seen in the eye.’ He is identified with the आत्मन्. Obviously he cannot be the reflection seen in the eyeball. He is the person who animates the eye and enables it to see. Or he is the person seen through the inner eye after purifying the मिन्द् through disciplines like brahmacharya or celibacy. Actually he is the द्रष्टा, the seer and not दृश्य, the seen. He is ब्रह्मन्. meditation upon him as the seer or even as the eye that sees everything else is Akṣipuruṣavidyā. The fruits of such meditation are believed to be obtaining all good things, shining in all worlds and after death, not being reborn.
See also VIDYĀS.
